BUDGET MANAGEMENT
In fiscal 2026, the World Bank Group evolved its budget
processes to enhance transparency and efficiency.
These reforms established a more integrated budget
framework across IFC, MIGA, and the World Bank,
linking business planning, workforce planning,
and budget decisions more directly to institutional
priorities and development outcomes. They simplified
planning and reporting processes, improved visibility
of total resources, and introduced stronger tools for
management oversight. The reforms also streamlined
cost-sharing arrangements, improved the treatment
of donor and external funding, reduced some clientfacing fees, and strengthened financial forecasting
and revenue visibility. They further supported financial
sustainability by creating efficiencies and redeploying
resources to fund strategic priorities.

We have fully embraced AI tools at the World Bank
Group, and we support clients to adopt, adapt, and
then advance them for their own needs. Our client
engagements focus on Small AI — affordable, fitfor-purpose solutions designed for local conditions,
including places with limited power, connectivity,
and computing capacity. This is not a second-best
path. It is a practical way to strengthen workers,
help firms grow, improve services, support local
entrepreneurs, and create more and better jobs.
There is much more to do, and no institution
can meet the jobs challenge alone. But this
year demonstrated what is possible when our
shareholders, clients, partners, and staff work
together with urgency and purpose.
The World Bank Group is faster, simpler, and
better equipped to deliver. Now we must build
on that progress — and help create more jobs for
more people.

The Executive Directors support the World Bank
Group’s urgent response to these crises while
maintaining a resolute focus on the long-term
challenge of creating jobs at scale. The Board is
encouraged that countries can increasingly access
fast-acting finance for emergency response,
with 79 countries to date utilizing Crisis Toolkit
Arrangements. In fiscal 2026, the Board reaffirmed
its support for the World Bank Group’s strategic
drive to create more and better-paid jobs as total
World Bank Group commitments for the year
reached $123.5 billion.1
The Board welcomes the World Bank Group’s
new ways of working. By deepening collaboration
across our institutions, we are enhancing
efficiency and accelerating our impact on the
ground. Forging new alliances with private
sector partners and clients and strengthening
cooperation with development partners ensures
that scarce resources are deployed where they can
generate the most jobs and growth.

The World Bank Group continues to evolve its internal
operations for the benefit of clients. The goal: to be
easier to work with, more present in the markets that

AND RESULTS
Three years ago, the World Bank Group launched its reform agenda
with a clear ambition: to become a faster, simpler, more effective,
and impactful institution — one better equipped to meet the scale and
urgency of today’s development challenges.
That agenda is now delivering results:
• Private capital mobilization
Public capital alone is not enough to tackle the world’s most pressing
development challenges. That’s why we mobilized $112 billion in private
funds in fiscal 2026 — more than triple the $35 billion mobilized in fiscal
2022 — to further expand opportunity, create jobs, and build infrastructure.
We also issued $25 billion in guarantees this year — surpassing our goal of
issuing $20 billion annually by 2030 — to give investors the confidence to
invest in developing countries.

In our own supply chain, we leverage the World Bank
Group’s purchasing power through a category-based
approach to maximize efficiency and value, including
by focusing on job creation through small businesses
and local sourcing. We also keep operations running
smoothly by identifying and addressing risks from
approximately 22,000 vendors globally.

The World Bank Group is the first multilateral
development bank to deploy a blockchain-based
platform for traceability of funds at the country level,
strengthening transparency and accountability in
fiduciary management. This initiative aligns with
the World Bank Group’s broader commitments to
digitalization and operational efficiency.

Over the past several years, IFC has been shifting
its model to not only deploy its own capital but to
mobilize more private capital from partners. That
shift is reflected in our fiscal 2026 results. The World
Bank Group mobilized $112 billion in private capital
in fiscal 2026, more than tripling from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022. IFC contributes to that outcome through
a range of instruments and products — guarantees,
originate-to-distribute structures, catalytic equity,
syndications, anchor investments, transaction
advisory, and local-currency financing — each designed
to address specific barriers that have historically
constrained private investment in developing
economies. In fiscal 2026, IFC achieved a record
$105.6 billion in investment commitments, including
over $73.6 billion in private capital mobilized.
Those investments translate into real-world outcomes
for millions of people. The expected impact of IFC’s
portfolio in fiscal 2026 includes:

AND JOBS
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of
finance to a platform that channels global capital
flows into developing countries. Rather than
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and
our convening role to crowd private capital into the
most productive sectors for job creation. This means
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool
of global capital to development opportunities.
In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that
are already translating into results. While financing
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years,
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

Crucially, the World Bank
Group Scorecard is proving essential not only
in monitoring progress but in reinforcing
institutional accountability.
Mobilizing private capital at scale remained a
central priority for shareholders in fiscal 2026.
Through targeted investments, advisory services,
and robust risk mitigation instruments, the World
Bank Group has helped crowd in private financing
for infrastructure, agribusiness, manufacturing,
and services — sectors that are indispensable for
job creation. The Board welcomes the closing of
the second securitization transaction under the
IFC’s Emerging Markets Securitization Program,
which demonstrates the viability of the institution’s
originate-to-distribute model. Total private
capital mobilized during the fiscal year reached
$112 billion, underscoring the World Bank
Group’s growing role as a multiplier of
development finance.

with a clear ambition: to become a faster, simpler, more effective,
and impactful institution — one better equipped to meet the scale and
urgency of today’s development challenges.
That agenda is now delivering results:
• Private capital mobilization
Public capital alone is not enough to tackle the world’s most pressing
development challenges. That’s why we mobilized $112 billion in private
funds in fiscal 2026 — more than triple the $35 billion mobilized in fiscal
2022 — to further expand opportunity, create jobs, and build infrastructure.
We also issued $25 billion in guarantees this year — surpassing our goal of
issuing $20 billion annually by 2030 — to give investors the confidence to
invest in developing countries.

This more than
threefold increase represents a fundamental shift in
our ability to bring external capital into development
opportunities at scale, making us the largest mobilizer
of private capital among multilateral development
banks. Guarantees issued by the World Bank Group
Guarantee Platform grew by 46 percent in fiscal
2026. We are providing patient equity in markets
where early-stage capital is scarce and expanding
local-currency financing where foreign-exchange risk
would otherwise deter investment. We also began
piloting “originate-to-distribute” approaches to connect
institutional investors with emerging market assets at
greater scale. And we’re providing investors and ratings
agencies with historical data on the performance
of emerging market lending through the Global
Emerging Markets Risk Database. These practical
shifts are already supporting investment and jobs.

This year’s results show the progress we have
made. We delivered $123.5 billion in financing
to clients. We mobilized $112 billion in private
capital, more than triple the $35 billion we
mobilized in fiscal 2022. Altogether, that brought
our total financing and mobilization in developing
economies to well over $200 billion in fiscal 2026.
The growth was broad-based. Between fiscal 2022
and fiscal 2026, private capital mobilization nearly
tripled in lower-middle-income countries, from
$14 billion to $37 billion; more than quadrupled in
upper-middle-income countries, from $12 billion
to $50 billion; and increased by nearly 150 percent
across Africa, from $9 billion to $22 billion.

The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by
initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water
Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected
to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply.
The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly,
approximately 29,000 jobs, as well as advancing long-term job creation.
The World Bank Group is part of a pool of international lenders providing
financing for the project: In fiscal 2026, the Board approved an IFC loan of
up to $375 million. IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million
concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green
Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of
up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan
Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This
is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water
reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness.
The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our
Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments,
long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water
security, economic growth, and job creation.

role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched

repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. Finally,

World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across
all three pillars.

farms to access markets, finance, technology, and resilience tools.

yet many remain in poverty, relying on traditional farming methods

COUNTRY ENGAGEMENT
We are building a One World Bank Group client
coverage model that aligns public and private sector
solutions around jobs, growth, and private investment.
Our new approach is more efficient, outcome-focused,
and systematic in tapping private sector solutions
and will help countries tackle their development
challenges with greater speed, quality, and impact.
The centerpiece of this new approach is our
Country Partnership Framework (CPF) — the
key tool that guides our strategic engagement
with countries. CPFs typically span four to six
years, with a maximum duration of 10 years, to
align our support with a country’s development
goals and the World Bank Group Scorecard.

In fiscal 2026, we delivered 28 new CPFs that are
underpinned by five core diagnostics: Country
Climate and Development Reports, Country
Growth and Jobs Reports, Country Private Sector
Diagnostics, Poverty and Equity Assessments, and
Public Finance Reviews. From this data, we identify
three to five outcomes that support job creation,
and complementary public and private actions to
support the outcomes. With outcomes defined at the
intersection of three selectivity criteria — development
challenges, country development goals, and World
Bank Group comparative advantages — CPFs
serve as the primary vehicle for translating World
Bank Group targets and strategies into countrylevel action, delivering on client priorities through
complementary public and private solutions.

As of fiscal 2026, we have merged 88 country offices
to unify leadership across IFC, MIGA, and the World
Bank under a single Country Manager. We plan to
continue consolidating country offices to give clients
a single point of entry to the World Bank Group and
make it easier for them to work with us. We are also
decentralizing to better serve clients: Over the next two
years, two-thirds of operations staff will be based in the
regions they serve. This will enable them to respond
more effectively to local needs, accelerate decisionmaking, and strengthen collaboration across the
World Bank Group.

During the Spring Meetings in April 2026, the
World Bank Group launched the Small States
Strategy. Guided by select solutions underpinned
by the World Bank Group Jobs Framework, the Strategy
prioritizes interventions with the greatest potential
to support job creation and economic growth.
Support will be differentiated to reflect individual
country contexts, while using regional approaches,
aggregated procurement, capacity building, and
stronger partnerships to address scale constraints,
high transaction costs, and partner fragmentation.
Implementation is anchored in Country Partnership
Frameworks. The Strategy was informed by feedback
from small states gathered through consultations
and engagement, including at the annual Small States
Forum held alongside the World Bank Group Annual
Meetings in October 2025.
For more information, visit https://www.
worldbank.org/en/country/smallstates.

concerns with CAO, which reports directly to the IFC
and MIGA Boards of Executive Directors. For more than
25 years, CAO has worked to facilitate the resolution
of complaints in a fair, objective, and constructive
manner; enhance environmental and social project
outcomes; and foster public accountability and
learnings to improve IFC/MIGA’s environmental and
social performance. CAO’s Dispute Resolution function
helps resolve issues between affected people and
the institutions’ clients using a neutral, collaborative,
investigation of the Requests for Inspection from
Tanzania and Togo. Furthermore, the Panel is
investigating a project in Uganda and has completed

The tools backing this approach are concrete. The
Small Loan Guarantee Program has backed lending
across 34 IDA and European Commission eligible
countries with a focus on fragile and conflict-affected
states. The Frontier Opportunities Fund provides
early-stage equity in markets too early for conventional
investment. A new $100 million Concessional Capital
Window serves fragile middle-income countries and
refugee-hosting economies. And the IDA Private Sector
Window has been streamlined to deploy blended
finance faster. In Ukraine, blended concessional
finance contributions from development partners
have reached more than $1 billion this year and have
been instrumental in enabling IFC to take on greater
risk, which in turn mobilizes additional private capital.
Moreover, the Local Champions Initiative, an IFC
program designed to identify and support promising
local entrepreneurs, shows how these tools scale,
building a replicable pipeline of investable local firms.

for government officials with structured country

risk insights, and deeper interoperability with country

role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched
in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved
technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030.
This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority
that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus.
Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique
capabilities. First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations

roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards,

the World Bank Group expands access to finance through MIGA’s
guarantees and insurance, as well as partnerships created by the
World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across
all three pillars.

approach by using trust funds to provide guarantee
instruments that de-risk investments for both public

Renewable Energy Catalyst Trust Fund, the West Bank

private sector investments by guaranteeing higher-risk
projects and increasing investor confidence, particularly
in fragile and conflict-affected settings, while advancing
job creation and women’s economic empowerment.

these efforts by strengthening environmental, social,
and gender practices and broadening access to
guarantees for small businesses in low-income

its model to not only deploy its own capital but to
mobilize more private capital from partners. That
shift is reflected in our fiscal 2026 results. The World
Bank Group mobilized $112 billion in private capital
in fiscal 2026, more than tripling from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022. IFC contributes to that outcome through
a range of instruments and products — guarantees,
originate-to-distribute structures, catalytic equity,
syndications, anchor investments, transaction
advisory, and local-currency financing — each designed
to address specific barriers that have historically
constrained private investment in developing
economies. In fiscal 2026, IFC achieved a record
$105.6 billion in investment commitments, including
over $73.6 billion in private capital mobilized.
Those investments translate into real-world outcomes
for millions of people. The expected impact of IFC’s

The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), home of the World Bank Group Guarantee
Platform, provides guarantees to facilitate the flow of foreign investment in developing countries,
enabling the private sector to create jobs. Our mandate is to encourage investment into developing
member countries by providing non-commercial risk guarantees (political risk insurance, credit
enhancement products, and trade finance guarantees) to investors and lenders.
In fiscal 2026, MIGA marked a major milestone by
surpassing $100 billion in cumulative guarantees
issued since its founding in 1988. With just $366 million
of paid-in capital from member countries, MIGA has
steadily pursued its stated mission for nearly four
decades by providing guarantees to private investors.
This paves the way for private funds to flow to emerging
and developing economies, enabling job creation.

Finally, in fiscal 2026, we convened nine MDBs
and IFIs to sign a Disbursement Harmonization
Memorandum of Understanding to reduce
administrative burdens on borrowers. We also
launched a World Bank-hosted platform to centralize
information on MDB harmonization, making
collaboration more transparent and accessible
across participating institutions. And, furthering our
harmonization efforts, we committed with other MDBs
to work toward a common approach for measuring the
jobs impact of our operations, in coordination with the
International Labour Organization.
PRIVATE INVESTORS
The World Bank Group works with a diverse range of
private and institutional investors, including commercial
banks, insurance companies, asset managers, pension
funds, and sovereign wealth funds, to expand financing
for high-impact projects and strengthen private sector
development in emerging markets.

AND JOBS
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of
finance to a platform that channels global capital
flows into developing countries. Rather than
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and
our convening role to crowd private capital into the
most productive sectors for job creation. This means
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool
of global capital to development opportunities.
In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that
are already translating into results. While financing
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years,
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.
